chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad from Salih ibn Abi Hammad, raising it, said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) came to Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays to console him for the death of a brother of his named Abdul Rahman. So Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you were to be impatient, you would have fulfilled the right of the womb (kinship), and if you were to be patient, you would have fulfilled the right of Allah. Indeed, if you are patient, the decree is executed upon you and you are praised; and if you are impatient, the decree is executed upon you and you are blamed.'

Al-Ash'ath said to him: 'Indeed we are to Allah and indeed to Him we are returning.' So Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you know its interpretation?' Al-Ash'ath said: 'No. You are the peak and limit of knowledge.' He said to him: 'As for your saying 'Indeed we are to Allah', it is your acknowledgment of the Sovereignty. And as for your saying 'and to Him we are returning', it is your acknowledgment of the destruction/death.'
ai.seo_question: What is the deeper interpretation of 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: In this narration from Al-Kafi, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) consoles Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays by distinguishing between the social duty of kinship fulfilled through grief and the spiritual duty to Allah fulfilled through patience. He further elucidates the theological depth of the phrase 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un', interpreting the first part as an acknowledgment of divine sovereignty (Al-Mulk) and the second as an admission of mortality and return to the Creator. This highlights the Shia emphasis on conscious, theological reflection during moments of personal loss.
